thread.title: Equities Fall As Apple Pressured By Trade War

author: Nasdaq
title: Equities Fall As Apple Pressured By Trade War
text:
Shutterstock photo Thursday, January 3 , 2019, 11:57 AM, EST NASDAQ Composite -1.96% Dow -2.38% S&P 500 -1.77% Russell 2000 -0.84% NASDAQ Advancers: 771 Decliners: 1532 AAPL -9% CELG +26% DAL -8.9% DNDN +4.2% Market Movers
ADP Employment +271k versus 157k in November Weekly Unemployment claims 231k, the most since the end of November Challenger Job Cuts 35.3% down from 51.5% on November ISM Manufacturing 54.1, the lowest in two years Construction Spending data delayed due to Federal Government shutdown Steve's Commentary
The markets opened in the red today with the major indices off over 1% each and have since moved to session lows. Despite the red, one interesting development is the small & midcap laden Russell 2000 index that outperformed yesterday and is holding up better today than the large cap stocks. The R2K led on the way down, so perhaps it is offering a glimmer of hope.
Apple tops the morning headlines after lowering revenue guidance for the first time in nearly 20 years. A significant slowdown in China gets much of the credit, and that can be taken as an indication that the trade war and the resulting slowdown in China's economy are taking a toll. On analyst commented that it is the scale of the slowdown in China that caught investors by surprise rather than the preannouncement itself.
Apple shares opened with an 8.8% decline, and should that hold through the close it marks the stock's largest one-day percentage drop in over 25 years. The White House Counsel of Economic Advisers warns that Apple might be the first but it won't be the last to see earnings decline due to headwinds with China.
Today's economic calendar offers a somewhat brighter outlook. ADP Employment data was the best since 2017 with 271k new positions added in December, well above expectations and November's revised 157k. In its release ADP stated the gains were broad based spanning most industries and shared across large, medium and small employers.
Going forward a Bloomberg News survey of economist says that employment gains will slow this year to a 156k monthly average and about 120k next year. The declines are reflective of full employment as well as a moderating economy, and survey respondents expect the national unemployment rate will fall to 3.5% by year's end. Tomorrow's Nonfarm payrolls of about 180k are expected, up from November, and the unemployment rate should hold steady.
Also out today is December ISM Manufacturing coming in at 54.1, a two-year low and below expectations of 57.5 and down from November's 59.3. Although readings above 50.0 reflect expansion, the major components making up the top ISM number also declined with new orders the lowest in five years and production down to 2012 levels. Bear in mind that ISM is survey based, with declining equities and dysfunction in DC likely having a subtle impact.
On the M&A front Bristol-Myers Squibb announced a $74 billion acquisition of Celgene, the largest pharmaceutical acquisition ever. Both firms compete in the competitive cancer treatment space, but investors might be a little wary. Celgene shares are soaring 26% and but still below the proposed takeover price while Bristol-Meyers is lower by 12.5%.
Crude oil prices are slightly positive but gave up earlier gains. This comes despite a Wall Street Journal report suggesting that two-thirds of fracking wells are consistently producing less oil that initially expected. Treasury yields are a little firmer with the 10-year at 2.567%. That comes as traders now expect the Fed will either hold rates at current levels or perhaps even cut a quarter point by year's end. Dallas Fed President Kaplan suggested that the Fed should holding steady for the next few quarters.
The sector view is negative of course with the only positive sector being REITs with a 0.9% advance. Technology leads the market decline with a 4.6% drop, the most since October 10th.

Brian's Technical Take
File this in the "meaningless stat of the day" bucket but yesterday the Nasdaq Composite closed at 6,665.94. And so it missed closing at 6,666 by 6 bps. That is a lot of 6's and reminds me of the Great Recession low for the S&P 500 index, 666.79, made on March 31st 2009. This time around we can't be so lucky as yesterday's close represents what looks like the closing high of the "dead cat bounce" off the 2018 low made last Monday, December 24th.
December 24th had the markings of a capitulation type flush which we highlighted last week in the breadth measures of the small cap Russell 2000. It was the worst Christmas eve on record and the same weak breadth measures can be seen in the Nasdaq Composite. On December 24th just 9% of the index was trading below its 200-day moving average, the lowest since 2009. In the prior session 35% of the index made new 52-week lows which was the lowest seen since October and November 2008.
Back then and despite a ring fenced housing market, Lehman Brothers went bankrupt, financials were restricted from short sales, the largest financial institutions were injected with capital, along with a host of other government programs in order to save the system. Today we have a global slowdown but the US economy has been running strong, financials are well capitalized, and credit is not at the forefront of concerns.
Liquidity appears to be a big problem and more complex than I can expand on, but I do wonder if we will look back on these times and say the Federal Reserve's two-pronged approach of raising rates and reducing the balance went too far, too fast. While 2018 does not appear to be anything like 2008, I suspect the Fed is not far from letting things get too much worse from here.
It is one thing to be wrong, and it is quite another to stay wrong. If a policy mistake was made and markets now need an injection of liquidity in some form, let's have it. While the Fed is forecasting two more hikes in 2019, markets are now pricing in a 94% probability they do nothing. And with the front end of the curve inverted, some are forecasting a rate cut by 2020.
For the Nasdaq Composite it has already made a near exact 50% Fibonacci Retracement of its 2016 - 2018 uptrend. While last week's low was accompanied by extreme breadth readings, we have yet to see the bullish divergences. It looks like we may be embarking on a retest of the 2018 low, if not lower. On that move I will be watching for improving breadth in the aforementioned measures, as well as momentum. The Composite's weekly RSI bottomed at 30 the week ending Friday, 12/21. Let's see if that level holds.
